def units_mod(f: int) -> List[int]:
    """The unit group (Z/f)^x as a sorted list of representatives."""
    return [u for u in range(1, f) if gcd(u, f) == 1]


def power_subgroup(f: int, q: int) -> List[int]:
    """The subgroup of q-th powers inside (Z/f)^x."""
    return sorted({pow(u, q, f) for u in units_mod(f)})


def residue_degree(f: int, q: int, u: int) -> int:
    """Order of the class of u in (Z/f)^x / ((Z/f)^x)^q: the residue degree."""
    powers: set = set(power_subgroup(f, q))
    d: int = 1
    v: int = u % f
    while v not in powers:
        v = (v * u) % f
        d += 1
    return d


def septic_type(p: int) -> int:
    """Residue degree of the prime p in the septic subfield of Q(zeta_29)."""
    return residue_degree(29, 7, p % 29)


def demo_splitting_law() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("1.  The septic subfield of Q(zeta_29): the splitting law")
    print("=" * 72)
    seventh_powers = power_subgroup(29, 7)
    print(f"  seventh powers mod 29        : {seventh_powers}")
    fourth_roots = [u for u in units_mod(29) if pow(u, 4, 29) == 1]
    print(f"  fourth roots of unity mod 29 : {fourth_roots}")
    assert seventh_powers == fourth_roots == [1, 12, 17, 28]
    print("  => u is a seventh power mod 29  <=>  u^4 = 1   (C_28 / C_4 = C_7)")

    degrees = {u: residue_degree(29, 7, u) for u in units_mod(29)}
    assert set(degrees.values()) <= {1, 7}
    split = sorted(u for u, d in degrees.items() if d == 1)
    print(f"  totally split classes        : {split}   (density {len(split)}/28 = 1/7)")
    print(f"  inert classes (degree 7)     : {28 - len(split)}/28 = 6/7")

    primes = [p for p in range(2, 400) if all(p % k for k in range(2, int(p**0.5) + 1))]
    sample = [p for p in primes if p != 29][:18]
    print("\n  prime : p mod 29 : residue degree")
    for p in sample:
        print(f"  {p:5d} : {p % 29:8d} : {septic_type(p):d}")
    for p in primes:
        if p != 29:
            predicted = 1 if p % 29 in (1, 12, 17, 28) else 7
            assert septic_type(p) == predicted
    print("  (splitting criterion verified for every prime below 400)")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Full pinning and the type entropy
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def type_entropy(q: int) -> float:
    """H(T) = log2 q - ((q-1)/q) log2 (q-1) for the degree-q rung."""
    return log2(q) - ((q - 1) / q) * log2(q - 1)


def demo_full_pinning() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("2.  Full pinning: the Frobenius class determines the type")
    print("=" * 72)
    us = units_mod(29)
    quartic_class = lambda u: tuple(sorted((u * h) % 29 for h in [1, 12, 17, 28]))
    ent = uniform_entropy(us, lambda u: residue_degree(29, 7, u))
    cond = conditional_entropy(us, lambda u: residue_degree(29, 7, u), quartic_class)
    info = ent - cond
    print(f"  H(T)                     = {ent:.10f} bits")
    print(f"  closed form log2 7 - (6/7) log2 6 = {type_entropy(7):.10f} bits")
    print(f"  H(T | Frobenius class)   = {cond:.10f}")
    print(f"  I(Frobenius class ; T)   = {info:.10f}  =  H(T)")
    assert abs(ent - type_entropy(7)) < 1e-12
    assert cond < 1e-12
    print("  => the channel is FULLY PINNED: capacity attained, no leakage.")
    print(f"  certified bracket 0.5916 < H(T) < 0.5918: {0.5916 < ent < 0.5918}")


def demo_quartic_character() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("3.  The quartic character carries ZERO information (CRT orthogonality)")
    print("=" * 72)
    # exponent (discrete-log) model: a runs over Z/28, type sees a mod 7 only
    exps = list(range(28))
    septic = lambda a: 1 if a % 7 == 0 else 7
    quartic = lambda a: a % 4
    ent = uniform_entropy(exps, septic)
    info = mutual_information(exps, septic, quartic)
    print(f"  H(T)  in the exponent model      = {ent:.10f} bits")
    print(f"  I(quartic character ; T)         = {info:.2e}   (exactly 0)")
    assert abs(info) < 1e-12
    for c in range(4):
        fib = [a for a in exps if a % 4 == c]
        counts = [sum(1 for a in fib if septic(a) == 1), sum(1 for a in fib if septic(a) == 7)]
        print(f"    fibre  a = {c} (mod 4):  split/inert counts = {counts}")
    print("  Every fibre of the quartic character has the same 1:6 type split,")
    print("  because gcd(4, 7) = 1 splits C_28 as C_4 x C_7.")


def demo_conductor_freeness() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("4.  Conductor-freeness of the degree-7 rung")
    print("=" * 72)
    print("  conductor f :   |(Z/f)^x| : split classes : H(T)")
    for f in (29, 43, 71, 113, 127, 197):
        us = units_mod(f)
        ent = uniform_entropy(us, lambda u: residue_degree(f, 7, u))
        n_split = sum(1 for u in us if residue_degree(f, 7, u) == 1)
        print(f"  {f:11d} : {len(us):10d} : {n_split:13d} : {ent:.10f}")
        assert abs(ent - type_entropy(7)) < 1e-12
        assert n_split * 7 == len(us)
    print("  Every prime conductor f = 1 (mod 7) gives the SAME entropy 0.5917 bits.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5-7.  The exponent box, the three channels, primality
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def ord_type(n: int, a: int) -> int:
    """Residue degree attached to the discrete-log class a: n / gcd(n, a)."""
    return n // gcd(n, a)


def type_pair(n: int, x: Tuple[int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Unordered pair of residue degrees of the two prime factors."""
    a, b = x
    u, v = ord_type(n, a), ord_type(n, b)
    return (min(u, v), max(u, v))


def split_count(t: Tuple[int, int]) -> int:
    """How many of the two prime factors split completely."""
    return (1 if t[0] == 1 else 0) + (1 if t[1] == 1 else 0)


def or_readout(t: Tuple[int, int]) -> int:
    """Does at least one of the two factors split completely?"""
    return min(split_count(t), 1)


def exponent_box(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    return [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]


def product_residue(n: int, x: Tuple[int, int]) -> int:
    """Discrete log of the semiprime N = p*q: a + b mod n."""
    return (x[0] + x[1]) % n


def I_pair(n: int) -> float:
    box = exponent_box(n)
    return mutual_information(box, lambda x: type_pair(n, x), lambda x: product_residue(n, x))


def I_split(n: int) -> float:
    box = exponent_box(n)
    return mutual_information(
        box, lambda x: split_count(type_pair(n, x)), lambda x: product_residue(n, x)
    )


def I_or(n: int) -> float:
    box = exponent_box(n)
    return mutual_information(
        box, lambda x: or_readout(type_pair(n, x)), lambda x: product_residue(n, x)
    )


def I_split_closed(q: int) -> float:
    """Closed form of the split-count channel at prime degree q."""
    p = 1.0 / q
    h_s = entropy_of_counts([(q - 1) ** 2, 2 * (q - 1), 1])
    h_cond = p * binary_entropy(1.0 / q) + (1 - p) * binary_entropy(2.0 / q)
    return h_s - h_cond


def I_or_closed(q: int) -> float:
    """Closed form of the OR channel at prime degree q."""
    h_or = entropy_of_counts([q * q - (2 * q - 1), 2 * q - 1])
    h_cond = (1.0 / q) * binary_entropy(1.0 / q) + ((q - 1.0) / q) * binary_entropy(2.0 / q)
    return h_or - h_cond


def demo_semiprime_law() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("5.  The semiprime split-count law at degree 7: Bin(2, 1/7)")
    print("=" * 72)
    box = exponent_box(7)
    counts = [sum(1 for x in box if split_count(type_pair(7, x)) == s) for s in (0, 1, 2)]
    print(f"  observed counts out of 49      : {counts}")
    print(f"  binomial law 49 * Bin(2, 1/7)  : {[36, 12, 1]}")
    assert counts == [36, 12, 1]
    print(f"  P(both split) = 1/49 = {1/49:.6f}   P(exactly one) = 12/49 = {12/49:.6f}")


def demo_channels() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("6.  The three channels at degree 7")
    print("=" * 72)
    isp, ior, ipair = I_split(7), I_or(7), I_pair(7)
    closed_isp = log2(7) + (30 * log2(5) - 78 * log2(3) - 78) / 49
    closed_ior = log2(7) + (30 * log2(5) - 66 * log2(3) - 13 * log2(13) - 54) / 49
    print(f"  Ipair(7)  (type pair)        = {ipair:.10f}")
    print(f"  Isplit(7) (split count)      = {isp:.10f}")
    print(f"  closed form                  = {closed_isp:.10f}")
    print(f"  G(7)      (OR read-out)      = {ior:.10f}")
    print(f"  closed form                  = {closed_ior:.10f}")
    assert abs(isp - closed_isp) < 1e-12 and abs(ior - closed_ior) < 1e-12
    assert abs(ipair - isp) < 1e-12
    print(f"  certified bracket 0.1140 < Isplit(7) < 0.1142 : {0.1140 < isp < 0.1142}")
    print(f"  certified bracket 0.01027 < G(7) < 0.01035    : {0.01027 < ior < 0.01035}")
    print(f"  reported anchor 0.1161 vs true value         : gap = {0.1161 - isp:.6f}")
    print(f"  ledger anchor 0.0103 identified as G(7)      : |G(7)-0.0103| = {abs(ior-0.0103):.6f}")
    print(f"  OR coarsening loses a factor  Isplit/G = {isp/ior:.3f}  (> 11)")
    print(f"  ladder monotonicity: Isplit(11) = {I_split(11):.6f} < Isplit(7) = {isp:.6f}")
    print(f"  anchor 0.116 sits nearer degree 7: "
          f"|Isplit(7)-0.116| = {abs(isp-0.116):.6f} < |Isplit(11)-0.116| = {abs(I_split(11)-0.116):.6f}")


def demo_primality() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("7.  Primality is exactly the sufficient-statistic condition")
    print("=" * 72)
    print("   n : prime? :   Ipair(n) :  Isplit(n) :    gap")
    for n in range(2, 13):
        ip, isp = I_pair(n), I_split(n)
        is_prime = n > 1 and all(n % k for k in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))
        print(f"  {n:2d} : {str(is_prime):6s} : {ip:10.6f} : {isp:10.6f} : {ip - isp:9.6f}")
        if is_prime:
            assert abs(ip - isp) < 1e-12
        else:
            assert ip - isp > 1e-9
    print("\n  Degree 4 in closed form:")
    print(f"    Ipair(4)  = 5/4                       = {I_pair(4):.10f}")
    print(f"    Isplit(4) = 19/8 - (21/16) log2 3     = {19/8 - (21/16)*log2(3):.10f}")
    assert abs(I_pair(4) - 1.25) < 1e-12
    assert abs(I_split(4) - (19 / 8 - (21 / 16) * log2(3))) < 1e-12
    print("    the type pair breaks the one-bit cap; the split count restores it,")
    print("    losing more than three quarters of the channel.")


def demo_asymptotics() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print("8.  The conjectural second-order decay law")
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"  target constants:  2 log2 e = {2*log2(2.718281828459045):.6f}, "
          f"log2 e - 1 = {log2(2.718281828459045)-1:.6f}")
    print("      q      q^2 Isplit(q) - log2 q      q^2 G(q)")
    for q in (7, 101, 1009, 10007, 100003):
        a = q * q * I_split_closed(q) - log2(q)
        b = q * q * I_or_closed(q)
        print(f"  {q:7d}   {a:22.6f}   {b:12.6f}")


def main() -> None:
    demo_splitting_law()
    demo_full_pinning()
    demo_quartic_character()
    demo_conductor_freeness()
    demo_semiprime_law()
    demo_channels()
    demo_primality()
    demo_asymptotics()
    print()
    print("All assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Anchor Audit and Certified Brackets: Confirming the OR Channel, Falsifying the Split-Count Figure
demos.description: Recomputes the two degree-seven channel values directly on the exponent box and checks them against their closed forms, then audits the round's two inherited numerical anchors: the figure 0.0103 is confirmed to be the OR channel G(7) = 0.0103060 to within six millionths, while the figure 0.1161, reported as the split-count channel, is falsified by more than 0.0018 bits against the true value 0.1141053. It further shows that a nearby figure 0.116 attributed elsewhere to the degree-eleven rung is more than thirty times closer to the degree-seven value. Every bracket is then re-derived exactly, without floating point, by clearing denominators and performing a single big-integer comparison; the script closes with the rescaled second-order asymptotics of the split-count channel at q = 7, 101, 1009, 10007 and 100003.
demos.code:
"""Anchor audit and asymptotics for the degree-seven rung.

This script does three things, all with exact arithmetic wherever possible:

  1. Recomputes the two closed-form channel values of the degree-seven rung
         I_split(7) = log2 7 + (30 log2 5 - 78 log2 3 - 78)/49
         G(7)       = log2 7 + (30 log2 5 - 66 log2 3 - 13 log2 13 - 54)/49
     directly from the exponent box, confirming the closed forms.

  2. Audits the two numerical anchors carried into the round: the figure 0.0103,
     which turns out to be the OR channel G(7), and the figure 0.1161, which was
     reported as the split-count channel and is falsified (true value 0.1141053).
     It also shows that a nearby figure 0.116, attributed elsewhere to the
     degree-eleven rung, is more than thirty times closer to degree seven.

  3. Verifies each bracket by a single big-integer comparison, so that no claim
     rests on floating-point evaluation.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import e, gcd, log2
from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Tuple

Point = Tuple[int, int]


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ entropy --
def entropy(counts: List[int]) -> float:
    total = sum(counts)
    return -sum((c / total) * log2(c / total) for c in counts if c > 0)


def tallies(points: List[Point], key) -> List[int]:
    d: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    for x in points:
        d[key(x)] = d.get(key(x), 0) + 1
    return list(d.values())


def mutual(points: List[Point], key, side) -> float:
    fib: Dict[Hashable, List[Point]] = {}
    for x in points:
        fib.setdefault(side(x), []).append(x)
    cond = sum((len(f) / len(points)) * entropy(tallies(f, key)) for f in fib.values())
    return entropy(tallies(points, key)) - cond


def box(n: int) -> List[Point]:
    return [(a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)]


def channels(n: int) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    pts = box(n)
    tau = lambda a: n // gcd(n, a)
    pair = lambda x: (min(tau(x[0]), tau(x[1])), max(tau(x[0]), tau(x[1])))
    scount = lambda x: (tau(x[0]) == 1) + (tau(x[1]) == 1)
    orbit = lambda x: min(int(scount(x)), 1)
    res = lambda x: (x[0] + x[1]) % n
    return (mutual(pts, pair, res), mutual(pts, scount, res), mutual(pts, orbit, res))


# -------------------------------------------------- exact bracket certifier --
def certify_greater(coeffs: Dict[int, Fraction], const: Fraction, bound: Fraction) -> bool:
    """Decide  sum c_m log2(m) + const > bound  by one big-integer comparison."""
    exps = dict(coeffs)
    exps[2] = exps.get(2, Fraction(0)) + const - bound
    denom = 1
    for f in exps.values():
        denom = denom * f.denominator // gcd(denom, f.denominator)
    lhs, rhs = 1, 1
    for base, f in exps.items():
        k = int(f * denom)
        if k > 0:
            lhs *= base ** k
        elif k < 0:
            rhs *= base ** (-k)
    return lhs > rhs


def main() -> None:
    ipair7, isplit7, g7 = channels(7)
    closed_isplit = log2(7) + (30 * log2(5) - 78 * log2(3) - 78) / 49
    closed_g = log2(7) + (30 * log2(5) - 66 * log2(3) - 13 * log2(13) - 54) / 49

    print("=== 1. closed forms at degree 7 ===")
    print(f"  I_pair(7)  = {ipair7:.10f}")
    print(f"  I_split(7) = {isplit7:.10f}   closed form {closed_isplit:.10f}")
    print(f"  G(7)       = {g7:.10f}   closed form {closed_g:.10f}")
    assert abs(isplit7 - closed_isplit) < 1e-12 and abs(g7 - closed_g) < 1e-12
    assert abs(ipair7 - isplit7) < 1e-12, "sufficiency at prime degree"

    print()
    print("=== 2. audit of the round's numerical anchors ===")
    print(f"  anchor 0.0103  vs  G(7)       : |diff| = {abs(g7 - 0.0103):.7f}  -> CONFIRMED (OR channel)")
    print(f"  anchor 0.1161  vs  I_split(7) : diff   = {0.1161 - isplit7:.7f}  -> FALSIFIED (> 0.0018)")
    isplit11 = channels(11)[1]
    print(f"  anchor 0.116   : |I_split(7)-0.116| = {abs(isplit7-0.116):.6f}, "
          f"|I_split(11)-0.116| = {abs(isplit11-0.116):.6f}  -> belongs to degree 7")
    print(f"  OR coarsening factor I_split(7)/G(7) = {isplit7/g7:.3f}")

    print()
    print("=== 3. brackets certified by integer comparison ===")
    forms = [
        ("H(T)      ", {7: Fraction(1), 6: Fraction(-6, 7)}, Fraction(0),
         Fraction(5916, 10000), Fraction(5918, 10000)),
        ("I_split(7)", {7: Fraction(1), 5: Fraction(30, 49), 3: Fraction(-78, 49)},
         Fraction(-78, 49), Fraction(1140, 10000), Fraction(1142, 10000)),
        ("I_split(4)", {3: Fraction(-21, 16)}, Fraction(19, 8),
         Fraction(29, 100), Fraction(30, 100)),
    ]
    for name, coeffs, const, lo, hi in forms:
        ok = certify_greater(coeffs, const, lo) and not certify_greater(coeffs, const, hi)
        print(f"  {name}: {float(lo)} < value < {float(hi)}  certified = {ok}")
        assert ok

    print()
    print("=== 4. the conjectured second-order law ===")
    def isplit_closed(q: int) -> float:
        h_s = entropy([(q - 1) ** 2, 2 * (q - 1), 1])
        hb = lambda p: -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)
        return h_s - ((1 / q) * hb(1 / q) + ((q - 1) / q) * hb(2 / q))
    for q in (7, 101, 1009, 10007, 100003):
        print(f"  q = {q:6d}:  q^2 I_split(q) - log2 q = {q*q*isplit_closed(q) - log2(q):.6f}"
              f"   (target 2 log2 e = {2*log2(e):.6f})")

    print()
    print("All assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Power-Residue Frobenius Descent: Computing Residue Degrees in the Degree-q Subfield of a Cyclotomic Field
algorithms.description: Given a prime conductor f, a degree q dividing f-1, and a prime p not dividing f, this algorithm returns the residue degree of p in the degree-q subfield of the f-th cyclotomic field. The mathematical foundation is that the subfield is the fixed field of the group of q-th powers in (Z/f)^x, so the Frobenius of p is the class of p modulo that subgroup and the residue degree is the order of that class. Two implementations are provided: a generic one that materialises the subgroup of q-th powers in one pass over the unit group, costing O(f log q) modular multiplications and then O(q) per query; and a fast test valid at prime degree, Euler's criterion p^((f-1)/q) = 1 mod f, costing O(log f) modular multiplications per query, which suffices because at prime degree the residue degree is either 1 or q. The routine also returns the totally split residue classes and their density, always exactly 1/q.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: prime conductor f, degree q with q | f-1, prime p with p not= f
OUTPUT: residue degree of p in the degree-q subfield K_q of Q(zeta_f)

1. U <- {u in [1, f-1] : gcd(u, f) = 1}                  // the unit group (Z/f)^x
2. P <- { u^q mod f : u in U }                            // subgroup of q-th powers, |P| = (f-1)/q
3. if q is prime then                                     // fast path
4.     if p^((f-1)/q) = 1 (mod f) then return 1 else return q
5. v <- p mod f ; d <- 1                                  // general path: order of the class pP
6. while v not in P do
7.     v <- v * (p mod f) mod f ; d <- d + 1
8. return d

COROLLARY (density): |P| = (f-1)/gcd(f-1, q) = (f-1)/q, so the totally split classes have
density exactly 1/q and the type entropy is log2 q - ((q-1)/q) log2 (q-1), independent of f.

algorithms.name: Exact Evaluation of the Splitting-Type Channels on the Exponent Box
algorithms.description: Computes the three semiprime channels of a degree n exactly. The exponent box is the set of pairs (a,b) with 0 <= a,b < n, carrying the uniform measure; the residue degree attached to an exponent is tau(a) = n/gcd(n,a); the hidden variable is either the unordered type pair, the split count in {0,1,2}, or the OR bit; and the observation is the product residue (a+b) mod n. Each channel value is the mutual information H(hidden) - H(hidden | observation), assembled from exact integer tallies so that the only floating-point operations are the final logarithms. The complexity is O(n^2 log n) time and O(n) memory, the log factor coming from the Euclidean algorithm. The output reproduces the exact identities of the theory: equality of the first two channels at every prime degree, the value 5/4 for the type-pair channel at degree 4, and the closed forms 0.1141053 and 0.0103060 at degree 7.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: degree n >= 2
OUTPUT: I_pair(n), I_split(n), G(n) in bits

1. B <- [(a,b) : 0 <= a < n, 0 <= b < n]                    // the exponent box, |B| = n^2
2. tau(a) := n / gcd(n, a)                                   // residue degree of one factor
3. Theta(a,b) := (min(tau a, tau b), max(tau a, tau b))      // unordered type pair
4. S(a,b) := [tau a = 1] + [tau b = 1]                       // split count in {0,1,2}
5. O(a,b) := min(S(a,b), 1)                                  // OR read-out
6. R(a,b) := (a + b) mod n                                   // product residue (the observation)
7. for each read-out X in {Theta, S, O}:
8.     H  <- entropy of the multiset { |X^{-1}(v)| : v in image X }
9.     Hc <- sum over r of (|R^{-1}(r)| / n^2) *
               entropy of { |X^{-1}(v) cap R^{-1}(r)| : v in image X }
10.    I(X) <- H - Hc
11. return I(Theta), I(S), I(O)

NOTE: all cardinalities are integers; entropy(c_1,...,c_k) = log2(sum c_i) - (1/sum c_i) *
sum c_i log2 c_i, so each channel value is a rational combination of logarithms of integers.

algorithms.name: Certified Bracketing of Logarithmic Channel Constants by Big-Integer Comparison
algorithms.description: Every channel value in this theory has the shape V = sum_i alpha_i log2(m_i) with rational coefficients alpha_i and small integer bases m_i. This algorithm decides an inequality V > L for rational L exactly, with no floating-point arithmetic: exponentiating turns the claim into a comparison of two products of integer powers, and clearing the common denominator D of all exponents makes those powers integral, so a single big-integer comparison settles it. This is the mechanism behind every certified bracket in the work: H(T) in (0.5916, 0.5918) reduces to 2^8283 * 6^12000 < 7^14000 < 2^8284 * 6^12000; the split-count channel at degree seven reduces to 2^16718 * 3^15600 < 7^9800 * 5^6000 < 2^16719 * 3^15600; and the one-bit cap at degree four reduces to the schoolbook bound 2^22 < 3^21. Complexity is dominated by one exponentiation and comparison of integers with O(D * L) bits, which is milliseconds for the brackets used here.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: coefficients {m_i -> alpha_i} (rationals), additive constant c (rational),
       rational bound L;  target V = c + sum_i alpha_i log2(m_i)
OUTPUT: the exact truth value of V > L

1. e_2 <- alpha_2 + c - L                       // fold the constant into the base-2 exponent
2. E   <- {m_i -> alpha_i} with entry for base 2 replaced by e_2
3. D   <- lcm of the denominators of all exponents in E
4. LHS <- product of m^(D * e) over entries with e > 0
5. RHS <- product of m^(-D * e) over entries with e < 0
6. return LHS > RHS                             // one big-integer comparison

CORRECTNESS: V > L  <=>  sum_i alpha_i log2 m_i + (c - L) > 0  <=>  prod_i m_i^alpha_i * 2^(c-L) > 1
<=>  (raising to the positive power D)  prod over positive exponents > prod over negative exponents.
A two-sided bracket lo < V < hi is decided by calling the routine twice.
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm C — Certified bracketing of a logarithmic constant by integer comparison.

Every channel value in this theory has the shape

        V = sum_i  alpha_i * log2(m_i),      alpha_i rational, m_i positive integers,

for instance  I_split(7) = log2(7) + (30 log2 5 - 78 log2 3 - 78)/49.  A claim
"V > L" with rational L is therefore equivalent, after clearing denominators by
the common denominator D, to a comparison of two products of integer powers:

        prod_i m_i^(D alpha_i)  >  2^(D L),

with all exponents integers (negative exponents are moved to the other side).
Deciding that inequality is a single big-integer comparison, so the bracket is
certified without any floating-point arithmetic.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import log2
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

# A logarithmic constant: {integer base: rational coefficient} plus a rational
# additive constant (i.e. a multiple of log2(2) = 1 is just the constant).
LogForm = Tuple[Dict[int, Fraction], Fraction]


def evaluate(form: LogForm) -> float:
    """Floating-point value, for orientation only."""
    coeffs, const = form
    return float(const) + sum(float(c) * log2(m) for m, c in coeffs.items())


def _integer_sides(form: LogForm, bound: Fraction) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (LHS, RHS) integers such that  V > bound  <=>  LHS > RHS."""
    coeffs, const = form
    exponents: Dict[int, Fraction] = dict(coeffs)
    exponents[2] = exponents.get(2, Fraction(0)) + const - bound  # V - bound as a log
    denom: int = 1
    for e in exponents.values():
        denom = denom * e.denominator // __import__("math").gcd(denom, e.denominator)
    lhs, rhs = 1, 1
    for base, e in exponents.items():
        k = int(e * denom)
        if k > 0:
            lhs *= base**k
        elif k < 0:
            rhs *= base ** (-k)
    return lhs, rhs


def certify_greater(form: LogForm, bound: Fraction) -> bool:
    """Exact decision of  V > bound  by one big-integer comparison."""
    lhs, rhs = _integer_sides(form, bound)
    return lhs > rhs


def certify_bracket(form: LogForm, lo: Fraction, hi: Fraction) -> bool:
    """Exact decision of  lo < V < hi."""
    return certify_greater(form, lo) and not certify_greater(form, hi)


def witness_sizes(form: LogForm, bound: Fraction) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Bit-lengths of the two integers actually compared."""
    lhs, rhs = _integer_sides(form, bound)
    return lhs.bit_length(), rhs.bit_length()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- examples ---
H_T_SEVEN: LogForm = ({7: Fraction(1), 6: Fraction(-6, 7)}, Fraction(0))
I_SPLIT_SEVEN: LogForm = (
    {7: Fraction(1), 5: Fraction(30, 49), 3: Fraction(-78, 49)},
    Fraction(-78, 49),
)
G_SEVEN: LogForm = (
    {7: Fraction(1), 5: Fraction(30, 49), 3: Fraction(-66, 49), 13: Fraction(-13, 49)},
    Fraction(-54, 49),
)
I_SPLIT_FOUR: LogForm = ({3: Fraction(-21, 16)}, Fraction(19, 8))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cases: List[Tuple[str, LogForm, Fraction, Fraction]] = [
        ("H(T) at degree 7 ", H_T_SEVEN, Fraction(5916, 10000), Fraction(5918, 10000)),
        ("I_split(7)       ", I_SPLIT_SEVEN, Fraction(1140, 10000), Fraction(1142, 10000)),
        ("G(7)             ", G_SEVEN, Fraction(1027, 100000), Fraction(1035, 100000)),
        ("I_split(4)       ", I_SPLIT_FOUR, Fraction(2947, 10000), Fraction(2948, 10000)),
    ]
    for name, form, lo, hi in cases:
        ok = certify_bracket(form, lo, hi)
        bits = witness_sizes(form, lo)
        print(f"{name}: value = {evaluate(form):.10f}   bracket ({float(lo)}, {float(hi)}) "
              f"certified = {ok}   witness sizes = {bits[0]} vs {bits[1]} bits")
        assert ok
    print("all brackets certified by exact integer comparison")

visualizations.name: The Decay of the Ladder: Three Channels Against Prime Degree, With Their Second-Order Law
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure. The left panel plots, on log-log axes and for every prime degree up to 200, the single-prime type entropy H(T) = log2 q - ((q-1)/q) log2 (q-1), the semiprime split-count channel and the OR channel, with the degree-seven rung marked and annotated (0.5917, 0.1141, 0.01031 bits) and the conjectured envelopes (log2 q + 2 log2 e)/q^2 and (log2 e - 1)/q^2 drawn as dashed guides. The visual message is the change of exponent: the single-prime channel decays like (log2 q)/q, the semiprime channels like 1/q^2. The right panel rescales the semiprime channels by q^2 and subtracts log2 q, showing both curves flattening onto the pure entropy-curvature constants 2 log2 e = 2.885390 and log2 e - 1 = 0.442695.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation 1 — The decay of the ladder.

Plots the three information quantities of the abelian splitting-type ladder as a
function of the prime degree q:

    H(T)      = log2 q - ((q-1)/q) log2 (q-1)          (single prime, fully pinned)
    I_split(q)                                          (semiprime, split count)
    G(q)                                                (semiprime, OR read-out)

together with the conjectured second-order asymptotics
    I_split(q) ~ (log2 q + 2 log2 e) / q^2 ,     G(q) ~ (log2 e - 1) / q^2 .

Produces `ladder_decay.png`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import e, log2
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def binary_entropy(p: float) -> float:
    if p <= 0.0 or p >= 1.0:
        return 0.0
    return -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)


def entropy_of_counts(counts: List[float]) -> float:
    total = sum(counts)
    return -sum((c / total) * log2(c / total) for c in counts if c > 0)


def type_entropy(q: int) -> float:
    return log2(q) - ((q - 1) / q) * log2(q - 1)


def conditional_term(q: int) -> float:
    return (1.0 / q) * binary_entropy(1.0 / q) + ((q - 1.0) / q) * binary_entropy(2.0 / q)


def i_split(q: int) -> float:
    return entropy_of_counts([(q - 1) ** 2, 2 * (q - 1), 1]) - conditional_term(q)


def g_or(q: int) -> float:
    return entropy_of_counts([q * q - (2 * q - 1), 2 * q - 1]) - conditional_term(q)


def primes_up_to(n: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (n + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = False
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def main() -> None:
    qs = primes_up_to(200)
    h = [type_entropy(q) for q in qs]
    isp = [i_split(q) for q in qs]
    g = [g_or(q) for q in qs]
    asym_split = [(log2(q) + 2 * log2(e)) / q**2 for q in qs]
    asym_g = [(log2(e) - 1) / q**2 for q in qs]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

    ax = axes[0]
    ax.loglog(qs, h, "o-", color="#3fb950", label=r"$H(T)$  (single prime, fully pinned)")
    ax.loglog(qs, isp, "s-", color="#58a6ff", label=r"$I_{\rm split}(q)$  (semiprime, split count)")
    ax.loglog(qs, g, "^-", color="#f0883e", label=r"$G(q)$  (semiprime, OR bit)")
    ax.loglog(qs, asym_split, "--", color="#1f6feb", lw=1,
              label=r"$(\log_2 q + 2\log_2 e)/q^2$")
    ax.loglog(qs, asym_g, "--", color="#9e5a26", lw=1, label=r"$(\log_2 e - 1)/q^2$")
    for q, y, txt in [(7, type_entropy(7), "0.5917"), (7, i_split(7), "0.1141"), (7, g_or(7), "0.01031")]:
        ax.annotate(txt, (q, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 6), fontsize=9)
    ax.axvline(7, color="#8b98a8", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set_xlabel("prime degree $q$")
    ax.set_ylabel("bits")
    ax.set_title("Three channels of the abelian ladder")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.semilogx(qs, [q * q * v - log2(q) for q, v in zip(qs, isp)], "s-", color="#58a6ff",
                label=r"$q^2 I_{\rm split}(q) - \log_2 q$")
    ax.axhline(2 * log2(e), color="#1f6feb", ls="--", lw=1, label=r"$2\log_2 e = 2.885390$")
    ax.semilogx(qs, [q * q * v for q, v in zip(qs, g)], "^-", color="#f0883e",
                label=r"$q^2 G(q)$")
    ax.axhline(log2(e) - 1, color="#9e5a26", ls="--", lw=1, label=r"$\log_2 e - 1 = 0.442695$")
    ax.set_xlabel("prime degree $q$")
    ax.set_ylabel("rescaled channel")
    ax.set_title("The conjectured second-order law")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    fig.suptitle("The abelian splitting-type ladder: exact values and their asymptotics", fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("ladder_decay.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote ladder_decay.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Exponent Box: Why Primality Is Exactly the Sufficient-Statistic Condition
visualizations.description: Side-by-side maps of the exponent box at degree 7 (prime) and degree 4 (the first composite degree). Each cell (a,b) is coloured by its type pair and labelled with its split count, and the fibres of the product residue (a+b) mod n are overlaid as diagonal point contours. At degree 7 only two residue degrees exist, so colour is a function of the split count alone and the two channels coincide at 0.114105 bits. At degree 4 the intermediate degree 2 appears: several distinct type pairs share the split count 0, the colouring is strictly finer than the labelling, and the channel collapses from the exact value 5/4 to 19/8 - (21/16) log2 3 = 0.294737 bits. The figure makes the combinatorial mechanism of the primality criterion directly visible.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualisation 2 — The exponent box: why primality is the sufficiency condition.

Draws the exponent box B_n = {(a,b) : 0 <= a,b < n} for n = 7 (prime) and n = 4
(the first composite degree), colouring each cell by its type pair, and overlays
the fibres of the product residue R = (a+b) mod n as diagonal contours.

At n = 7 only two residue degrees exist (1 and 7), so the colour is a function of
the split count alone: the split count is a sufficient statistic and the two
channels coincide.  At n = 4 the intermediate degree 2 appears, several distinct
type pairs share the split count 0, and the split-count channel collapses from
5/4 bits to 19/8 - (21/16) log2 3 = 0.2947 bits.

Produces `exponent_box.png`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, log2
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

PALETTE: List[str] = ["#3fb950", "#58a6ff", "#a371f7", "#f0883e", "#f85149", "#8b949e"]


def tau(n: int, a: int) -> int:
    return n // gcd(n, a)


def type_pair(n: int, a: int, b: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    u, v = tau(n, a), tau(n, b)
    return (min(u, v), max(u, v))


def split_count(n: int, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    t = type_pair(n, a, b)
    return (t[0] == 1) + (t[1] == 1)


def draw(ax, n: int) -> None:
    types = sorted({type_pair(n, a, b) for a in range(n) for b in range(n)})
    colour: Dict[Tuple[int, int], str] = {t: PALETTE[i % len(PALETTE)] for i, t in enumerate(types)}
    for a in range(n):
        for b in range(n):
            t = type_pair(n, a, b)
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((b, n - 1 - a), 1, 1, facecolor=colour[t],
                                       edgecolor="#0e1116", linewidth=1.2))
            ax.text(b + 0.5, n - 1 - a + 0.5, f"S={split_count(n, a, b)}",
                    ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color="#0b0f14")
    for r in range(n):
        pts = [(b + 0.5, n - 1 - ((r - b) % n) + 0.5) for b in range(n)]
        pts.sort()
        ax.plot([p[0] for p in pts], [p[1] for p in pts], ".", color="#0b0f14",
                markersize=3, alpha=0.35)
    ax.set_xlim(0, n)
    ax.set_ylim(0, n)
    ax.set_xticks([x + 0.5 for x in range(n)])
    ax.set_xticklabels(range(n), fontsize=8)
    ax.set_yticks([y + 0.5 for y in range(n)])
    ax.set_yticklabels(reversed(range(n)), fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("exponent $b$ of the second prime factor")
    ax.set_ylabel("exponent $a$ of the first prime factor")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor=colour[t], label=f"type {t}") for t in types],
              fontsize=8, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1.0))


def main() -> None:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))
    draw(axes[0], 7)
    axes[0].set_title("degree 7 (prime): colour = split count\n"
                      r"$I_{\rm pair}(7) = I_{\rm split}(7) = 0.114105$ bits", fontsize=11)
    draw(axes[1], 4)
    axes[1].set_title("degree 4 (composite): the type pair sees more\n"
                      r"$I_{\rm pair}(4) = 5/4$ vs $I_{\rm split}(4) = "
                      r"\frac{19}{8}-\frac{21}{16}\log_2 3 = 0.294737$", fontsize=11)
    fig.suptitle("The exponent box: primality is exactly the sufficient-statistic condition",
                 fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("exponent_box.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote exponent_box.png  "
          f"(check: log2-based value {19/8 - (21/16)*log2(3):.6f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Septic Oracle: One Residue Mod 29 Decides a Global Factorisation
interactive_demos.description: An interactive oracle for the degree-seven splitting law. Enter any integer (or draw a random prime) and the widget reports whether it splits completely in the septic subfield of the 29th cyclotomic field, together with its residue mod 29, its discrete logarithm base 2, that logarithm modulo 7, and its fourth power mod 29 — the four faces of the same criterion. A live SVG diagram places the 28 units mod 29 on a circle ordered by discrete logarithm, highlighting the four seventh powers {1, 12, 17, 28} that constitute the totally split classes and marking the user's input. A second panel runs over all primes below a user-chosen bound and displays the observed split density converging to the predicted 1/7, and a written panel explains why the seventh powers coincide with the fourth roots of unity and how this yields the type entropy 0.5916728 bits with full pinning by the Frobenius class and zero information from the quartic character.
interactive_demos.html:
The Septic Oracle

A prime p splits completely in the degree-7 subfield of the 29th cyclotomic field exactly when p mod 29 lies in {1, 12, 17, 28} — equivalently, when the discrete logarithm of p modulo 29 is divisible by 7. Type a number in and watch one residue decide a global factorisation.

The 28 units mod 29 on a circle, ordered by discrete logarithm base 2. Green spokes are the four seventh powers {1,12,17,28} — the totally split classes (density 1/7). Your number is the white ring.

Density counter

Run over the primes below a bound and watch the split fraction approach the predicted density 1/7 = 0.142857...

Why only four classes?

The units mod 29 form a cyclic group of order 28. Raising to the 7th power is a homomorphism whose image is the subgroup of order 28/gcd(28,7) = 4, and a unit u is a seventh power exactly when u^4 = 1. (If u = v^7 then u^4 = v^28 = 1; conversely if u^4 = 1 then (u^3)^7 = u^21 = (u^4)^5 u = u.) Solving x^4 = 1 mod 29 gives exactly {1, 12, 17, 28}. The quotient C28/C4 = C7 is the Galois group of the septic subfield, and the class of p in it is the Frobenius.

Consequence in bits: the type is 1 with probability 1/7 and 7 with probability 6/7, so its entropy is H(T) = log2(7) − (6/7)log2(6) = 0.5916727..., and knowing the Frobenius class removes all of it. The complementary C4-coordinate — the quartic character, which contains the quadratic residue symbol mod 29 — removes none of it: each of its four fibres contains exactly one split class and six inert ones.

interactive_demos.title: The Channel Ladder Explorer: How Many Bits Does a Semiprime Leak About Its Factors?
interactive_demos.description: A live laboratory for the three semiprime channels. A slider selects the degree n from 2 to 30; the widget builds the full n-by-n exponent box in the browser and computes, exactly, the type-pair channel, the split-count channel and the OR channel as mutual informations against the product residue. The box is drawn as a colour-coded grid — green where both factors split, blue where exactly one does, grey where neither does, and orange for the configurations involving an intermediate residue degree that only exist at composite degree — with an option to dim all cells outside a single fibre of the product residue so that the conditioning step becomes visible. A bar chart and a table report the three channel values, the split-count cell counts, the gap between the first two channels and the OR coarsening factor, and a commentary panel switches between the sufficiency message at prime degree (gap exactly zero) and the loss message at composite degree, quoting the exact degree-4 values 5/4 and 19/8 - (21/16) log2 3. Expandable notes give the precise definitions and the reason the equality holds exactly at prime degree.
interactive_demos.html:
The Channel Ladder Explorer

A semiprime N = p₁p₂ is modelled by the discrete logarithms (a,b) of its two prime factors in a cyclic Galois group of degree n. An observer sees only the residue of the product, i.e. a+b mod n. How many bits does that buy about the hidden splitting behaviour? Move the slider and find out — everything below is computed exactly from the n²-point exponent box.

both factors split (S=2) exactly one splits (S=1) neither splits (S=0) intermediate degree present

Row = exponent a, column = exponent b. Orange cells can only occur at composite n: they are the configurations whose residue degree is neither 1 nor n, and they are exactly what the split count forgets.

The three channels, in bits

What exactly is being computed?

Each point (a,b) of the box is equally likely. The residue degree attached to an exponent is tau(a) = n/gcd(n,a); the hidden variable is either the unordered pair (tau(a),tau(b)) (the type pair), the number S of coordinates with tau = 1 (the split count), or the single bit min(S,1) (the OR read-out). The observation is R = a+b mod n. Each channel value is the mutual information I = H(hidden) − H(hidden | R), computed with base-2 logarithms over the exact cell counts — no sampling, no approximation.

At prime degree the split count determines the type pair (residue degrees can only be 1 or n), so the first two channels are literally equal. At composite degree an intermediate degree n/d appears and the equality breaks: at n = 4 the type-pair channel is exactly 5/4 bits while the split-count channel is 19/8 − (21/16)log2(3) = 0.294737...

interactive_layout:
# One residue, seven primes: a guided tour of the splitting-type ladder Take a prime number $p$ and a number field $K$. Inside $K$ the prime $p$ may shatter into many smaller primes, or stay stubbornly whole. The classical miracle — [Artin reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_reciprocity_law) — says that for *abelian* $K$ this global behaviour is decided by a single local datum: the residue of $p$ modulo the conductor. This page turns that miracle into a number. How many **bits** does one residue buy you? And what happens to those bits when you look, not at a prime, but at a product of two primes — the situation an eavesdropper faces when handed a semiprime modulus? By the end you will be able to state and use: - the **degree-seven splitting criterion** for the septic subfield of the 29th cyclotomic field, - the **full pinning theorem** ($I = H(T)$, capacity attained) and its conductor-free generalisation, - the exact values of the **three semiprime channels**, and - the theorem that **primality of the degree is exactly the condition** under which "how many factors split" loses no information. --- ## 1. The oracle: one residue decides everything Let $\zeta_{29}$ be a primitive 29th root of unity. The Galois group of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{29})$ is $(\mathbb{Z}/29)^\times \cong C_{28}$, cyclic. Since $7 \mid 28$, there is a unique subfield $K_7$ of degree $7$: the fixed field of the subgroup of seventh powers. The seventh powers mod $29$ form a group of order $28/\gcd(28,7) = 4$, and a delightful coincidence identifies it concretely: $$u \text{ is a seventh power mod } 29 \iff u^4 = 1 \iff u \in \{1, 12, 17, 28\}.$$ > **Degree-seven splitting criterion.** A prime $p \neq 29$ splits completely in > $K_7$ — breaking into seven distinct primes — if and only if > $p \bmod 29 \in \{1, 12, 17, 28\}$. Otherwise it stays inert with residue > degree exactly $7$. There is no intermediate behaviour. Try it. Feed the oracle any number and watch the verdict, the discrete logarithm, and the position of your prime on the 29-clock. {{interactive_demo:0}}
Click to reveal the proof of the criterion Write $P = \{u^7 : u \in (\mathbb{Z}/29)^\times\}$. If $u = v^7$ then $u^4 = v^{28} = 1$ by Lagrange's theorem, since the group has order $28$. Conversely if $u^4 = 1$ then $$(u^3)^7 = u^{21} = (u^4)^5 \cdot u = u,$$ so $u \in P$. Hence $P = \{u : u^4 = 1\}$, and solving $x^4 = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/29$ gives $\{1,12,17,28\}$. The residue degree of $p$ is by definition the order of the class $pP$ in the quotient group $(\mathbb{Z}/29)^\times/P \cong C_7$. That order divides $7$, and $7$ is prime, so it is $1$ or $7$; it is $1$ precisely when $p \in P$.
The densities follow immediately: $4$ of the $28$ classes split, so a random prime splits with probability exactly $1/7$ and is inert with probability $6/7$. This is the source of every number on this page. --- ## 2. From densities to bits Uncertainty is measured by [entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)). A variable that is $1$ with probability $1/7$ and $7$ with probability $6/7$ has $$H(T) \;=\; \tfrac17\log_2 7 + \tfrac67 \log_2 \tfrac76 \;=\; \log_2 7 - \tfrac67 \log_2 6 \;=\; 0.5916727\ldots \text{ bits}.$$ Now the punchline. Do not look at $p \bmod 29$ itself — look only at its *coset* modulo $\{1,12,17,28\}$, a strictly coarser invariant with just seven values. That coset is precisely the Frobenius element of $p$ in $\mathrm{Gal}(K_7/\mathbb{Q})$. > **Full pinning at degree seven.** Conditioned on the Frobenius class, the > residue degree has *zero* remaining uncertainty: > $$H(T \mid \text{Frobenius}) = 0, \qquad I(\text{Frobenius}; T) = H(T) = 0.5916727\ldots$$ > The channel attains its capacity: nothing is lost and nothing is left over. Equally striking is the complementary statement. Because $C_{28} \cong C_4 \times C_7$ and $\gcd(4,7)=1$, the $C_4$-coordinate — the **quartic character**, which contains the ordinary quadratic residue symbol mod $29$ — is *completely blind*: > **Orthogonality.** $I(\text{quartic character}; T) = 0$ exactly. Each of the four > fibres of the quartic character contains exactly one split class and six inert > ones.
Why is the rung the same for every conductor? Nothing above used $29$ beyond the fact that it is a prime with $7 \mid 28$. In general, for primes $q$ and $f$ with $q \mid f - 1$, the $q$-th powers in the cyclic group $(\mathbb{Z}/f)^\times$ form the subgroup generated by $g^q$, of order $(f-1)/\gcd(f-1,q) = (f-1)/q$. Hence: * the splitting density is exactly $1/q$, and * the type entropy is $H(T) = \log_2 q - \frac{q-1}{q}\log_2(q-1)$, **independent of $f$**. So the degree-seven rung built over conductor $29$ and the one built over conductor $43$ carry literally the same $0.5917$ bits. The rung is an invariant of the *degree*, not of the field. Full pinning, remarkably, needs no hypothesis at all: for any modulus and any degree, the Frobenius class determines the residue degree, simply because the residue degree is a class function.
Here is the algorithm behind the oracle, including the fast Euler-criterion test. {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 3. Now multiply two primes together An eavesdropper is rarely handed a prime. They are handed a **semiprime** $N = p_1 p_2$ and asked to say something about the factors. Model this in logarithmic coordinates. Each factor is an exponent $a \in \mathbb{Z}/n$ in the cyclic Galois group of degree $n$, with residue degree $\tau_n(a) = n/\gcd(n,a)$; the two exponents are independent and uniform. The observer sees the product, whose exponent is $a + b \bmod n$. So we have an $n^2$-point **exponent box**, a hidden variable, and an observation. Three levels of resolution for the hidden variable give three channels: | hidden variable | channel | what it asks | |---|---|---| | the **type pair** $(\tau_n(a), \tau_n(b))$ | $I_{\mathrm{pair}}(n)$ | full splitting behaviour of both factors | | the **split count** $S \in \{0,1,2\}$ | $I_{\mathrm{split}}(n)$ | how many factors split completely | | the **OR bit** $\min(S,1)$ | $G(n)$ | does at least one factor split? | Drag the slider and watch all three, computed exactly on the box. Pay attention to what happens when the degree switches between prime and composite. {{interactive_demo:1}} At degree $7$ the split count follows the binomial law $\mathrm{Bin}(2,1/7)$ *exactly*: of the $49$ configurations, $36$ have no split factor, $12$ have one, and $1$ has two. The channels evaluate to $$I_{\mathrm{split}}(7) = \log_2 7 + \frac{30\log_2 5 - 78\log_2 3 - 78}{49} = 0.1141053\ldots,$$ $$G(7) = \log_2 7 + \frac{30\log_2 5 - 66\log_2 3 - 13\log_2 13 - 54}{49} = 0.0103060\ldots$$ Compare with $H(T) = 0.5917$ for a single prime. Multiplying two primes destroys about $80\%$ of the signal; collapsing the count to a single bit destroys more than $90\%$ of what remains ($11\,G(7) < I_{\mathrm{split}}(7)$).
Click to reveal why the OR channel can never beat the split count Fix the product residue $r$. If $r = 0$ the fibre contains exactly one point with $S = 2$ and $q-1$ points with $S = 0$; if $r \neq 0$ it contains exactly two points with $S = 1$ and $q - 2$ with $S = 0$. Either way, **inside a single fibre $S$ takes at most one non-zero value**, so on that fibre $S$ and $\min(S,1)$ induce the same partition and therefore the same conditional entropy. Since the conditional entropies are equal, the two channels differ *exactly* by their unconditional entropies: $$I_{\mathrm{split}}(q) - G(q) = H(S) - H(\min(S,1)) \ge 0,$$ the inequality being the standard fact that a function of a variable has no more entropy than the variable. This is a data-processing inequality obtained from an exact identity rather than an estimate.
Here is the exact channel evaluator used by the widget. {{algorithm:1}} --- ## 4. Primality is exactly the sufficiency condition Look again at the widget with $n$ prime versus $n$ composite. At every prime degree the top two bars are *identical*; at every composite degree they separate. That is not a numerical accident. > **Sufficiency at prime degree.** If $q$ is prime the only possible residue > degrees are $1$ and $q$, so the number of split factors already determines the > whole unordered type pair. Hence $I_{\mathrm{pair}}(q) = I_{\mathrm{split}}(q)$. > **Primality is the exact condition.** For every $n \ge 2$, the split count > induces the same partition of the exponent box as the full type pair **if and > only if $n$ is prime**.
Click to reveal the composite counterexample and the degree-4 computation If $n = de$ with $1 < d < n$ and $e \ge 2$, then $\tau_n(d) = n/d = e$ while $\tau_n(1) = n$. The two configurations $(d,d)$ and $(1,1)$ both have split count $0$, yet their type pairs are $(e,e)$ and $(n,n)$ — different. The split count records *how many* trivial degrees occur and forgets *which* non-trivial degrees occur; that datum is empty precisely when the divisor lattice of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ has a single non-trivial level, i.e. precisely when $n$ is prime. At $n = 4$ everything is computable by hand. The type pair takes six values with cell sizes $1,2,4,1,4,4$ out of $16$, giving $H(\Theta) = 19/8$ and, after conditioning on the product residue, $H(\Theta \mid R) = 9/8$. Hence $$I_{\mathrm{pair}}(4) = \frac{19}{8} - \frac{9}{8} = \frac54,$$ a *rational* channel value, and one that exceeds the one-bit cap obeyed by every binary read-out. The split count has cells $(9,6,1)$ and gives $$I_{\mathrm{split}}(4) = \frac{19}{8} - \frac{21}{16}\log_2 3 = 0.2947367\ldots < 0.3,$$ so more than three quarters of the channel is destroyed — and the cap is restored. The strict inequality follows from the schoolbook integer bound $2^{22} < 3^{21}$, which gives $\log_2 3 > 22/21$ and hence $I_{\mathrm{split}}(4) < 19/8 - 11/8 = 1$.
This picture makes the mechanism visible: the coloured cells of the exponent box are the type pairs, and the extra colours that appear at composite degree are exactly the information the split count throws away. {{visualization:1}} --- ## 5. The ladder, and where it is going Assembling all degrees gives a ladder of channels, each rung a different question asked of the same arithmetic. The single-prime rung decays like $(\log_2 q)/q$; the semiprime rungs decay like $(\log_2 q)/q^2$. {{visualization:0}} The right-hand panel shows a conjecture that the exact closed forms make irresistible: $$q^2\,I_{\mathrm{split}}(q) = \log_2 q + 2\log_2 e + O(1/q), \qquad q^2\,G(q) \to \log_2 e - 1 = 0.442695\ldots$$ Both channels are second-order Taylor remainders of the same binary entropy, so the leading constants are pure *entropy curvature* — $\log_2 e$ — carrying no arithmetic information about the field whatsoever. The arithmetic sits entirely in the $\log_2 q$ term. --- ## 6. Trust, but certify Every quantity here is a finite combination of logarithms of small integers. That has a practical consequence: any claimed decimal can be *decided* exactly. The trick is to clear denominators and compare two whole numbers. For example, $H(T) > 0.5916$ at degree seven is equivalent to $$2^{8283}\cdot 6^{12000} < 7^{14000},$$ and $I_{\mathrm{split}}(7) > 0.1140$ is equivalent to $$2^{16718}\cdot 3^{15600} < 7^{9800}\cdot 5^{6000}.$$ {{algorithm:2}} This mattered. Two numerical anchors were carried into this rung from earlier experimentation, and the closed forms settle both: - the figure $0.0103$ is **confirmed** — but as the *OR* channel, $G(7) = 0.0103060$; - the figure $0.1161$, advertised as the split-count channel, is **falsified**: the true value is $0.1141053$, short by more than $0.0018$ bits, far outside any rounding; - and a nearby figure $0.116$ attributed elsewhere to the *degree-eleven* rung is more than thirty times closer to degree seven ($0.1141$) than to degree eleven ($0.0519$) — the signature of a mislabelled rung. Run the audit yourself: {{demo:1}} --- ## 7. The whole story in one run Finally, here is the complete numerical companion: the splitting law, the densities, full pinning, the orthogonality of the quartic character, conductor-freeness across five different conductors, the $\mathrm{Bin}(2,1/7)$ law, all three channels with their closed forms, the primality scan for $n \le 12$, and the asymptotics. {{demo:0}} --- ## Where to read more - [Cyclotomic fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_field) and their subfields — the source of every example here. - [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem) — why "density $1/7$" is a theorem about primes and not just about residues. - [Mutual information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_information) and the [data processing inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing_inequality). - [Sufficient statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufficient_statistic) — the concept whose arithmetic incarnation turned out to be primality of the degree. **The one-sentence summary.** For a single prime, one residue is a perfect oracle worth $0.5917$ bits; for a product of two primes the same residue is worth $0.1141$ bits, for a yes/no question $0.0103$ bits — and the reason we may say "split count" instead of "full splitting type" throughout is precisely, and only, that the degree is prime.
